title: Global load balancing: send users to the nearest healthy region
caption: DNS (or anycast) chooses the region; each region's load balancer then spreads load inside it.

steps.text: The resolver asks GeoDNS, which answers with the address of the closest region that passes its health checks.
European users land on the EU load balancer, which spreads them over EU servers: ~20 ms away instead of ~150 ms.
The EU region fails. DNS starts answering with the US address, and new connections fail over. Clients holding a cached answer wait out the TTL, so keep it short (30–60 s).
Each regional LB is itself a redundant pair or cluster with a floating IP, so the LB is never the single point of failure.

scenarios.name: Region outage
scenarios.summary: GeoDNS health checks notice the dead region and answer with the other one; users pay extra latency instead of an outage.

steps.text: The whole EU region goes dark: power, network or a bad deploy.
GeoDNS health checks fail for EU, so new lookups get the US address.
European users now cross the Atlantic: ~150 ms instead of ~20 ms, but they are served.
The US region must have the headroom (and the data) for EU's traffic, or the failover takes it down too.

scenarios.name: Stale DNS cache
scenarios.summary: DNS failover is only as fast as the TTL, and some resolvers ignore it. Keep TTLs short and expect a tail of users on the old address.

steps.text: A user resolved the name a minute ago and cached the EU address for its 300 s TTL.
EU fails. GeoDNS already answers US, but this client never asks again until its cache expires.
Until then its requests keep failing. Some resolvers and apps cache even longer than the TTL.
Mitigation: TTL of 30–60 s, client retry with re-resolve, or anycast so the IP itself never changes.

scenarios.name: Alternative: anycast
scenarios.summary: One IP announced from every region; BGP routes each user to the nearest edge. Failover takes seconds, with no DNS caching, but it needs your own network.

steps.text: Every user connects to the same IP address. Internet routing (BGP) delivers the packets to the nearest point of presence.
European packets reach the EU edge and go to the EU region.
EU fails and stops announcing the route. Within seconds BGP sends the same IP to the US: no DNS TTL to wait out.
Trade-off: needs your own IP space and BGP (or a provider like Cloudflare or a cloud global LB), and long TCP sessions can break when routes shift.
